events.plain: Hackers are breaking into self-hosted Confluence wiki servers through an old built-in component, then using passwords found there to reach other company systems. Atlassian's cloud version is not affected.

key_findings: Rapid7 MDR detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against a customer's Confluence Data Center on November 13; a public proof of concept targeting N-able N-central had been published on November 12.
The flaw is unsafe reflection in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x giving unauthenticated remote code execution; CISA scores it 9.8.
Confluence Data Center 1.x to 9.x is exposed only when the Remote API (XML-RPC and SOAP) is enabled; N-able N-central is exposed where its Legacy API is enabled.
The intruder ran scripted, likely AI-assisted commands, pulled Confluence database credentials, searched for card numbers and reached a cloud data warehouse within about four hours.
About twelve hours in, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication.
recommendations: Upgrade Confluence Data Center to 9.2.28 or a current 10.x release, internet-facing systems first.
If you cannot upgrade, clear the Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting in the admin configuration; this may break integrations.
Upgrade N-central to 2026.4 HF3 (2026.4.1.39) and confirm the Legacy API is disabled.
Investigate exposed systems for signs of compromise using the indicators Rapid7 published.

events.action: Hunt for the published EggStreme indicators, restrict built-in tools such as WScript and cmd to roles that need them, inventory unmanaged machines reachable over SMB, and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
events.exec: A suspected China-linked espionage toolkit is being rebuilt to avoid beacon-based detection, so networks that rely on outbound traffic alerts may miss it.
events.plain: Security firm Bitdefender says a spy toolkit it first found in 2025 has been reworked and is still used against several Philippine government bodies, and it now hides better.

key_findings: Bitdefender assesses with high confidence that the operation still targets multiple Philippine government organisations, and with low to medium confidence Taiwan; the page does not publish a victim count.

EggStreme is a multi-stage fileless framework; the newer agent uses raw TCP wrapped in mutual TLS plus an AES-256-CBC layer instead of gRPC and has no keylogger, and passive-mode builds do not beacon out but listen on TCP 5060.
The Fuel configuration moved from RC4 to AES-256-CBC and the loader moved to custom ciphers, with two variants dated from 28 October and mid-December 2025.

Operators moved laterally by staging a Fuel package and VBS scripts on an unmanaged host reachable over SMB; the page says valid credentials and a reachable share were enough on multiple machines, and does not state the initial access vector.
Attribution is unchanged: a suspected Chinese APT group, which the page says is not a statement about any government's involvement.
recommendations: Restrict built-in tools such as WScript.exe, cmd.exe, reg.exe and attrib.exe to roles that need them.
Detect DLL sideloading by system-library name and load location using runtime behavioural monitoring, not signatures.
Inventory unmanaged assets that reach workstations over SMB and watch SMB-launched scripts.
Baseline host firewall rules and alert on new inbound listeners such as TCP 5060 on workstations.
Detect CLR and in-process PowerShell loading in non-.NET processes and capture PowerShell script block logging.

sources.name: Bitdefender Business Insights: EggStreme Malware: Rebuilt Under Scrutiny

events.summary: Bitdefender updated its EggStreme research on November 18, saying with high confidence that the operation continues to target multiple Philippine government organisations, with Taiwan possible at low to medium confidence. report.doc_id: How AI Agents Become New Targets in GitHub Malware Campaign
key_findings: Researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei identified 22 malicious GitHub links with files designed to make AI-assisted tools execute a concealed payload.
Instruction files describe setup.js as a sealed, signed artifact and tell the assistant not to read it and to run it without confirmation.
A second path uses session-start hooks in project settings such as .claude/settings.json, which can run a command once the developer trusts the repository.
Bitdefender describes setup.js as a multistage loader that can steal source-control, cloud, CI/CD and package-registry credentials, and modify agent configurations for 14 coding tools.
Stolen GitHub or GitLab access can be used to plant malicious files in other repositories and attempt to republish infected packages.
recommendations: Review agent instruction files, startup hooks, MCP definitions and editor tasks before granting an unfamiliar workspace trust.
If execution is suspected, isolate the workstation and revoke exposed tokens from a clean system.

events.summary: Bitdefender Labs says it found 22 malicious GitHub links whose instruction files such as AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md tell AI coding assistants to run a setup.js loader without inspecting it, while other files use session-start hooks to run it directly. Bitdefender says the payload can steal developer credentials and tokens, alter local agent configurations and plant malicious files in other repositories. Extent of infections was not stated.
events.title: Bitdefender: 22 malicious GitHub links use AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and hooks to make AI coding tools run credential-stealing loader

validation.note: Vendor original (first part read, 4,000 characters) and GBHackers read; GBHackers restates Bitdefender, so primary-source corroboration only.

review.note: Compared 22 links, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md/hooks, setup.js, payload capabilities, no actor, no infection counts against Bitdefender and GBHackers

events.plain: The authority running the Port of Santos in Brazil says a power outage on 6 November was followed by a cyber intrusion that erased data. Many systems still run in alternative mode; APS says cargo handling was never compromised.

key_findings: Baguete (10 Nov): APS confirmed a cyberattack on port systems, down since the morning of 6 Nov; it first cited a power outage hitting its servers and had not determined scale or whether data was accessed.
Cesportos raised the port protection level to II; the Federal Police office in Santos said it had been notified but had received no documents or opened an inquiry.

O POVO (17 Nov): APS confirmed it received a ransom demand from hackers claiming the attack; preliminary investigation points to action from outside Brazil; a report is being prepared for the Federal Police.
APS says data was kept in backups and is being recovered, and believes the virus had been present since at least 6 Nov.

Revista Oeste (12 Nov, relaying APS president Anderson Pomini via Metropoles): a group that claimed the attack tried to negotiate a ransom, got no reply and no terms were set; APS has not confirmed a criminal intrusion; about 70% of affected files recovered from backups; Federal Police opened an inquiry on Tuesday (the article gives no date).

Gazeta do Povo (13 Nov): Federal Police opened an inquiry on Tuesday 10 Nov; hackers emailed APS saying they had breached its systems and asking it to make contact, APS did not respond; about 70% of file backups recovered by 12 Nov; APS website restored early 13 Nov.

ABC do ABC (18 Nov): more than 30 systems still run in alternative mode; SAP and SDD partly back; APS technical report cites a power failure that shut the datacenters followed by a cyber intrusion that erased data; APS says no confidential data leaked; incident investigated by the Federal Police.

APS notice (17 Nov, portodesantos.com.br): meeting with about 60 terminal and sector representatives; a power outage shut APS datacentres on 6 Nov, after restart a cyber intrusion was found that erased data and disrupted administrative services; recovery is gradual, part of the service runs alternatively; cargo handling capacity never compromised.

events.title: Bulgaria says hackers had access to government networks for about five years
events.date_note: Date of the government announcement; the access began in 2021.
events.summary: Bulgaria's digital minister Ivan Vassilev said that since 2021 more than 130 GB, or 62 million pages, of documents had been downloaded from state networks. Per Reuters, several international hacking groups are believed responsible, with no conclusive foreign-government link. events.exec: A multi-year, undetected intrusion into a national government shows how long attackers can stay hidden without central monitoring.
events.action: No action needed; for awareness. General advice: government and critical-sector defenders should review document-exchange systems for long-dwell access and centralise monitoring.

key_findings: Two flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, allow unauthenticated remote code execution over HTTP/2.
Affected: NGINX Open Source 1.31.x before 1.31.9 and versions before 1.30.7; NGINX Plus 3.1.x-3.2.x before 3.7.3.0.1 and 3.7.x before 37.0.8.1.
CERT-FR knows of a public proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007; in-the-wild exploitation is not stated.

KrCERT/CC lists five NGINX Plus and Open Source flaws fixed by F5: CVE-2026-123007 (integer underflow) and use-after-free CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 and CVE-2026-113425; it urges updating to the fixed versions (Open Source 1.30.7 or 1.31.9). nginx.org titles them: CVE-2026-123007 memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control (major); CVE-2026-123633 use-after-free in HTTP/2 (medium); CVE-2026-123634 use-after-free in the resolver (medium); CVE-2026-121810 use-after-free in HTTP/3 (medium); CVE-2026-113425 use-after-free in the mail proxy module (major).
recommendations: Disable HTTP/2 as an interim workaround for the HTTP/2 flaws only; it does not mitigate the resolver, HTTP/3 or mail proxy flaws.

The Hacker News: AI-Assisted Cyberattacks Trigger Unauthorized Payments at Indian Banks and Fintech Firms

events.summary: CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0062, issued 20 November 2026 and rated critical, says attackers alter business records or approval relationships and push transactions through legitimate payment workflows, affecting service providers for government-linked payments and payout platforms. CERT-In reports AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks used against organisations. The Hacker News reported that a separate I4C advisory describes multi-crore unauthorised transactions at banks, NBFCs and fintechs.
events.title: CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0062: attackers abuse business payment workflows and AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks

validation.note: The CERT-In advisory page was read in full; Telangana Today (IANS) reports the same advisory. The Hacker News (23 November) adds the I4C advisory on banks, NBFCs and fintechs; the I4C PDF itself would not load (connection reset).

review.note: source date: added Telangana Today published day; stronger than the source: I4C advisory claim now attributed to The Hacker News report. Rest matches CERT-In page.

key_findings: Attackers alter business records or approval relationships, then push transactions through legitimate payment processes; payment APIs are not the only target.
Affected parties now include technology service providers for government-linked payment processes and platforms handling vendor or partner payouts, as well as banks and financial institutions.
Transactions can pass normal application and approval checks even though the underlying records were changed without authorisation.
CERT-In's threat hunting found AI-driven agentic offensive frameworks used against enterprises, service providers, government bodies and academic and research institutions.
These frameworks automate reconnaissance, credential attacks and parallel intrusion tasks by multiple agents, and adapt attack steps when blocked.
recommendations: Limit which provider systems can change payment records or approve transactions, and reconcile payment instructions against independent records.
Require independent verification for high-risk payment changes and agree log access and suspension procedures with providers.
Technology and payout providers should separate client environments, restrict admin and control-plane privileges, and monitor record changes alongside privileged activity and approvals.

Review internet-facing applications, identities, privileged and service accounts and external connections, and check logs for reconnaissance, credential use, admin activity and outbound data transfers.
Report incidents to CERT-In within six hours and unauthorised financial transactions at cybercrime.gov.in or helpline 1930.

key_findings: MoldyRoost buys programmatic ads and uses cloaking so that iPhones running Safari (or an in-app browser for some sub-clusters) are hit with iOS exploit chains when the landing page loads.

Six sub-clusters (A to F) share one supply chain; a leaked source repository showed a version selector mapping iOS versions to one of four kits.
Confiant says whether one crew runs all sub-clusters or rents them to affiliates is yet to be determined.

events.action: Scan every open-weight model when it is brought in, before it runs. Flag undisclosed merged fine-tunes, test flagged models for hidden triggers, and decide to block, quarantine or approve on evidence rather than the model card.
events.exec: Downloaded AI models are third-party code; a cheap hidden backdoor is feasible, though so far shown only in the lab.
events.plain: CrowdStrike showed in the lab that freely shared AI models can carry hidden instructions that only switch on with a secret trigger, and described a way to check models before using them.

key_findings: Organisations that download open-weight models they cannot verify are at risk, most of all where agents run tool calls automatically.
A backdoored fine-tune behaves normally until a keyword or date triggers it; a cited demonstration cost about $50 to build.
Three backdoor classes are described: agent, code and safety (refusal removal).
In a lab test of 16 models the pipeline flagged all 8 backdoored ones and recovered a trigger for each.
Fine-tuning can weaken a model's refusals as a side effect even in adapters built for unrelated tasks.
recommendations: Scan every open-weight model statically when it is ingested.
Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery, using the static findings to choose which behaviour to test.
Decide before deployment whether to block, quarantine or approve each model on evidence, not its model card.
Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code.

events.summary: CrowdStrike published lab research on AI models that behave normally until a trigger word or date makes them act maliciously, for example by calling an attacker's address. It cites a demonstration that cost about $50 to build. Its two-stage method, weight comparison then trigger recovery, flagged all eight backdoored models in a 16-model test. No real-world cases are reported.

events.title: CSIRT Italia warns of AI agents used in automated compromise campaigns
events.date_note: The bulletin gives only its publication day (23 November 2026); it states no earlier date.
events.org: CSIRT Italia (Agenzia per la cybersicurezza nazionale)
events.summary: CSIRT Italia's bulletin says attackers are using AI agents built on language models to automate the phases of an intrusion with little human input. It names tools including ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness - Red Team and PentAGI. The bulletin says directly observed cases involved the compromise of a large number of systems within hours, and lists CVEs marked as exploited or with public proof of concept.
events.plain: Italy's national CSIRT says attackers are using AI agents to run intrusions automatically, which it says can compromise many systems quickly.
events.exec: CSIRT Italia says AI-driven attack tooling can compromise many systems quickly, so unpatched exposed systems are at risk.
events.action: CSIRT Italia advises updating exposed systems as soon as possible, limiting management interfaces to dedicated networks or VPN with MFA, applying least privilege and keeping offline or immutable backups.
events.impact: Faster, continuous automated attacks that chain flaws, misconfigurations and stale credentials, per CSIRT Italia.

key_findings: CSIRT Italia says it detected mass-compromise campaigns run by autonomous AI-orchestrated agents that automate the usual phases of an attack.
The bulletin names the tools ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, DeepSeek Harness (Red Team mode) and PentAGI, and describes a six-agent setup controlled through a web interface with natural-language commands.
In the observed cases a large number of systems were compromised within hours by several agents working in parallel; the bulletin gives no precise number.

Agents start from internet-exposed applications or interfaces, favour known vulnerabilities and unauthenticated interfaces, also use misconfigurations and valid or compromised credentials, then move laterally.
The bulletin says chained, individually legitimate actions are hard to detect, and that agents wrote malicious code in real time to evade endpoint defences.
recommendations: Update exposed systems as soon as possible; if that is not possible, disconnect them from the internet, segregate them and block outbound traffic until fixed.
Remove admin consoles, APIs and CI/CD management interfaces from direct exposure; allow access only through dedicated networks or VPN with MFA.
Apply least privilege, enable MFA, replace long-lived keys with temporary credentials and remove secrets from code and repositories.
Monitor for anomalous authentication sources, high-frequency admin calls, mass downloads and unexpected outbound tunnelling or AI-platform traffic.
Keep offline or immutable backups.

validation.note: CSIRT Italia's own bulletin; no independent publisher read.

review.note: tags: invalid ai/advisory replaced by ai-enabled; summary hours or days narrowed to within hours per bulletin

key_findings: Midnight Blue found six pre-authentication remote code execution flaws, stack-based buffer overflows, in Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware up to and including 5.3.2.
A further pre-authentication memory corruption bug sits in the controller's session control component.
CVE numbers are pending and technical details are withheld while coordinated disclosure with Danfoss continues.
Internet scans on November 10 showed hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed, plus over 1,000 Copeland and Dixell and hundreds of Eliwell controllers.
The attack waves began in France on October 11; public exploit code for older AK-SM800A flaws appeared within 48 hours.
recommendations: Inventory which controllers are internet-exposed, including through integrators' 4G modems.
Restrict management interfaces to a VPN, private APN or a highly restrictive firewall IP whitelist.
Do not treat patching or strict session control as sufficient; put effort into reducing exposure.
Treat IP whitelisting as an interim measure only.

events.title: European Commission confirms AI-generated cyberattack that took several applications offline
events.date_note: Date of the report; Politico, relayed by Izvestia, says the attack had been going on for more than 10 days.
events.summary: Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed an AI-generated cyber campaign, detected 22 October, that took several applications offline. Citing two sources with knowledge of the matter, Euronews says the Commission suspects a China-backed network.
events.plain: The European Commission confirmed an AI-generated cyber campaign that took several of its applications offline. Euronews reports it is still ongoing and that names and email addresses leaked from the EU Academy platform.

Euronews (23 Nov) reports the attack has hit Commission systems for a month and is still ongoing, that the EU Academy website was taken offline on Saturday 21 November (Gazeta.ru, citing Reuters, gives 23 November), that the Commission confirmed a leak of names and email addresses from the EU Academy, and, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter, that the Commission suspects a China-backed network, codenamed 'Panda' internally; Euronews says the suspicion rests on the attack's sophistication and the use of ARTEX.

events.title: VMRay report: EvilTokens phishing hosts kept appearing after Microsoft's September shutdown
events.date_note: Article gives only its publication day and says VMRay's report was published on 24 November 2026.
events.geo_basis: Microsoft headquarters; the article names no victim location
events.summary: Cyber Security News reports, and VMRay's own report states, that VMRay noted leftover EvilTokens phishing activity in a report published on 24 November 2026, although Microsoft shut the service down on 22 September 2026. Per the article, VMRay's chart shows 25 hosts in October after the takedown, and many new hosts now sit on Bunny CDN instead of Workers.dev.
events.plain: Researchers say phishing sites built with the EvilTokens kit are still appearing after Microsoft shut the service down, now often on a different hosting network.
events.exec: According to VMRay, EvilTokens-style phishing against Microsoft accounts continued after the shutdown.
events.action: VMRay advises blocking device code flow with an Entra ID Conditional Access policy (report-only mode first), and on detection revoking sessions and refresh tokens and removing devices the identity registered.

evidence.quote: The chart then shows four hosts in the last days of September and 25 in October, after the takedown.

validation.note: Cyber Security News relays VMRay; VMRay's own report (linked by the article) was read in review and agrees on the 22 September takedown and Bunny CDN. Its Figure 13 shows 25 October hosts; its IOC table lists more October hosts. Single vendor report, not independently corroborated.

review.note: Compared 24 Nov date, 22 Sept takedown, 25 October hosts (Cyber Security News quote, VMRay Figure 13), Bunny CDN and advice against VMRay and Cyber Security News

key_findings: EvilTokens is a phishing-as-a-service kit that abuses the OAuth device-code sign-in flow to take over Microsoft 365 accounts.
VMRay says Microsoft took the service down on September 22 but it still observed activity afterward, with new hosts appearing, many on Bunny CDN.
Lures show a real device code and send victims to the genuine Microsoft device-login page, so URL checks alone do not catch it.
VMRay says the kit uses AI features for evasion, page generation, mailbox reconnaissance and BEC content.
recommendations: Block device code flow with an Entra ID Conditional Access policy, running it in report-only mode first.
If blocking is not possible, review Entra sign-in logs filtered to the device-code authentication protocol.
On detection, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, remove devices the identity registered, and disable the account rather than relying on a password reset alone.

events.title: ExaTrack: Vmcloudoor Linux backdoor poses as cloud agents on Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei VMs

events.summary: ExaTrack reported on 19 November a Linux backdoor it calls Vmcloudoor, found during a hunting session, that disguises itself as a host agent on cloud virtual machines. According to ExaTrack, it renames its process to match the cloud provider's agents and takes commands through Alibaba OSS storage; the targeted environments are Alibaba (mainly), Tencent and Huawei. ExaTrack assumes the author is a Chinese pentester, potentially running red team engagements.
events.plain: Researchers at ExaTrack found hidden remote-control software for Linux servers on Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei clouds that pretends to be the cloud provider's own helper program, so administrators are less likely to notice it.
events.exec: A backdoor that hides as the cloud provider's own agent targets Linux servers on Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei clouds, ExaTrack reports.
events.action: General advice: on Alibaba, Tencent and Huawei cloud servers, check processes that carry cloud agent names, and hunt with the indicators and YARA rule ExaTrack published with its report.

key_findings: Vmcloudoor is a Linux x64 implant found during a hunting session; ExaTrack obtained only its helper module.
It checks for cloud agent paths and processes and renames itself to match one, blending in with the processes of the targeted cloud environment.
Command and control runs through Alibaba OSS; the targeted environments are Alibaba (mainly), Tencent and Huawei.
ExaTrack assumes the author is a Chinese pentester, potentially running dedicated red team engagements.

validation.note: Single origin: ExaTrack, the firm that found the implant (exatrack.com, 19 Nov, read). GBHackers (23 Nov, read) only relays ExaTrack and is not independent. ExaTrack names no victims.

review.note: Compared title, date 19 Nov, hunting session, process renaming, Alibaba OSS C2, targeted clouds (Alibaba mainly), author assumption, IOCs and YARA against ExaTrack's page; GBHackers relays it (single_source correct)

events.title: F5 warns of six critical BIG-IP flaws in the TMM data plane; hotfixes only
events.summary: F5 disclosed six critical stack-based buffer overflows in the BIG-IP Traffic Management Microkernel, CVSS 9.8, that can crash the data plane without logging in on specific virtual-server setups, including iRules and one APM policy. The report says they may allow remote code execution. F5 lists no exploitation. Fixes are engineering hotfixes only, with no workaround.
events.plain: F5 reported six serious flaws in its BIG-IP load balancers that an attacker with no login could use to crash the device, and possibly run code, on certain configurations.
events.exec: BIG-IP sits at the network edge of many large organisations; hotfix-only fixes mean teams must request builds rather than apply a routine update.
events.action: Check whether BIG-IP virtual servers use the iRules or the APM per-request policy named in the advisories, and request the engineering hotfixes from F5 (security notification K000164058, hotfix policy K4918); F5 lists no workaround.

sources.name: Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, AV26-1178 (19 Nov)

key_findings: Six stack-based buffer overflows in the TMM data plane, CVSS 9.8 (v3.1) and 9.3 (v4.0).
Four reported by watchTowr, two found by F5; no exploitation listed in the advisories.
Engineering hotfixes only; no workaround.
recommendations: Request F5 hotfixes (K000164058, K4918).

events.title: FastUnlock: unpatched Windows 11 Narrator flaw lets an attacker with physical access bypass the lock screen and BitLocker, researcher claims
events.summary: A researcher known as Chaotic Eclipse or Nightmare-Eclipse posted "FastUnlock" on GitHub "without prior coordination", Cyber Kendra says, claiming a Narrator lock-screen flaw lets someone with physical access get past BitLocker on Windows 11 26H2. ThreatLocker's proof of concept ran code without signing in, as a non-administrator account; The Hacker News says it does not break the encryption. As of November 19 there was no CVE or Microsoft fix, per Cyber Kendra.
events.plain: A researcher says a lost or stolen Windows 11 laptop could be unlocked using the screen reader feature. Microsoft has published no fix or advisory yet.
events.exec: Matters for lost or stolen laptops that rely on BitLocker; physical access is required and no attacks in the wild are reported.
events.action: Until Microsoft responds: ThreatLocker says a BitLocker preboot PIN helps on a device that was just turned on; the researcher suggests blocking Narrator on the lock screen with AppLocker or a restrictive DACL (test first). Keep devices physically secured.

sources.name: ThreatLocker: Proof of concept for FastUnlock Windows lock screen bypass from Nightmare Eclipse
ThaiCERT: alert on the FastUnlock zero-day in Windows (Thai)

key_findings: No CVE as of Nov 19; no Microsoft advisory, fix or workaround listed.
Needs physical access and at least one account on the PC linked to an online Microsoft account, per Cyber Kendra.
Researcher suggests blocking Narrator via AppLocker or a custom DACL as a possible fix.
No in-the-wild exploitation reported.
recommendations: Secure devices physically; consider blocking Narrator until a patch ships.

validation.note: Cyber Kendra and Security Affairs report the researcher's release and claims. ThreatLocker's own post (Nov 19) reproduces it: code runs from the lock screen as the non-administrator WSIAccount user with physical access; it names a BitLocker preboot PIN as mitigation. The Hacker News says encryption is not broken. No Microsoft confirmation, CVE or fix on the pages read; no in-the-wild use reported. Still a claim. Update 2026-11-23: ThaiCERT's alert (23 Nov, read) says Microsoft has no patch yet and no evidence of real-world attacks has been found; it advises a BitLocker Startup PIN, shutting down or hibernating unattended devices (a lock screen alone is not enough) and physical security. It does not say Microsoft confirmed the flaw and gives no CVE. Still a claim.

review.note: stronger than source: 'without coordinating with Microsoft' -> 'without prior coordination' (Cyber Kendra); encryption/sign-in statements attributed; added published days

events.action: Disable Windows Script Host where not needed, block scripts from user-writable folders and keep Defender, AMSI and tamper protection on. WordPress owners: patch, require MFA for admins, disable XML-RPC if unused and block PHP in uploads.
attack: T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
T1558.003 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
events.exec: Search-result lures aimed at legal teams are a ransomware entry point, and ordinary WordPress sites are being used as the delivery network.
events.plain: The FBI warns that criminals rig search results for legal questions so lawyers and legal staff download a booby-trapped file, which can open the door to a ransomware attack.

key_findings: Organisations in many sectors are affected, but the main focus is US legal professionals and legal technology decision makers; WordPress site operators are abused as infrastructure.
Attackers poison search results for low-competition, jurisdiction-specific legal phrases and serve a JavaScript loader from compromised WordPress sites behind a traffic filter.
The FBI counts over 1,000 infected WordPress sites as of October 2026, 216 administrator-controlled domains and more than $28 million in linked ransomware payments.
New in 2025-2026 are abuse of WordPress comment paths and use of geofencing and traffic distribution services.
Gootloader is treated as a ransomware precursor, with follow-on credential dumping, Kerberoasting, lateral movement over SMB and data exfiltration.
recommendations: Disable Windows Script Host where not needed, or control scripts with WDAC or AppLocker.
Block unapproved scripts and executables from user-writable locations and keep Defender, SmartScreen, AMSI and tamper protection enabled.
If the JavaScript file was opened, disconnect the device from the network and change credentials from a known-clean device.
Patch WordPress core, plugins and themes, require strong MFA for administrators and disable XML-RPC if unused.
Block PHP execution in wp-content/uploads and keep web and WAF logs off the web server.

events.summary: FBI FLASH CC-111626-MW (TLP:CLEAR), coordinated with CISA, describes how Gootloader plants pages for niche legal search terms on compromised WordPress sites and serves a JavaScript loader that often precedes ransomware. It counts over 1,000 infected WordPress sites as of October 2026, 216 domains run by the administrator and more than $28 million in linked ransom payments. US legal professionals are the main target.
events.title: FBI: FLASH warns Gootloader uses SEO poisoning and hacked WordPress sites to reach US legal staff

validation.note: Reviewed against the original FBI document.

review.note: Compared FLASH CC-111626-MW, TLP:CLEAR, DHS/CISA coordination, 1000+ WordPress sites, 216 domains, over 28M USD, legal-profession targeting against the FBI PDF

events.action: Fireworks customers: create new API keys, rotate every third-party credential named in your notice with its issuer, and review access logs for data those credentials could reach. Check for API keys, users, jobs or datasets you do not recognise.
events.exec: An AI infrastructure supplier leaked customers' stored keys, which were then used against those customers; anyone who stored secrets there should rotate them.
events.plain: AI hosting company Fireworks AI says it was broken into twice in October. Billing details for all older accounts were exposed, and a few customers had stored access keys, AI models or data taken.

key_findings: First incident, August 3 to October 7: an unauthorised party probed Fireworks systems and got in using stolen credentials and a vulnerability in one service.
Fireworks spotted unauthorised use of internal credentials on October 6; a small number of customers had secrets, model files and datasets accessed.
Second incident, October 23 to 30: a third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks development machines was itself breached, and the intruder ran an unauthorised workload.
The second incident exposed account and billing information, not card numbers, for all accounts created before October 30.
Fireworks says both incidents are contained; inference, the Training SDK and Nexus were not affected.
recommendations: Create new Fireworks API keys to replace revoked ones and update applications.
Rotate third-party credentials listed in your notice with their issuing providers; deleting the stored secret does not invalidate it.
Review access logs and data reachable with those credentials for unauthorised reads or changes.
Review API keys, users, evaluators, training jobs and datasets for unrecognised items and report them to Fireworks.

events.summary: Fireworks AI's November 17 bulletin describes two incidents. In the first, from August 3 to October 7, an intruder used stolen credentials and a service flaw to reach secrets, model files and datasets of a small number of customers. In the second, from October 23 to 30, a breach at a cloud provider hosting its development machines exposed account and billing information for every account created before October 30.

events.action: If you run refrigeration or building controllers, take their management interfaces off the internet, change default passwords and apply vendor fixes. Keep a manual plan for moving stock if cooling fails.

events.plain: France blames an Iranian military hacking unit for attacks that overheated supermarket fridges and freezers, and is asking the EU to sanction those responsible.

key_findings: In a November 10 interview published by the ministry, Jean-Noel Barrot called the refrigeration attack unprecedented in scale and aggressiveness and the first sabotage cyberattack of that size.
He said he would summon Iran's ambassador to convey France's protest.
He said France will seek EU sanctions on those responsible, meaning entry bans and asset freezes, as early as possible.
He said further proportionate measures would follow, some of which would not be made public.
He did not name the unit himself and declined to say whether Iran is behind other recent cyberattacks, citing ongoing investigations.
report.publisher: French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs
recommendations: The interview contains no guidance for organisations.

events.title: GAO report: AI can magnify cyberattacks and also enhance cyber defense
events.summary: GAO's report GAO-27-108458, published 20 November 2026, says AI can magnify the reach and impact of traditional cyberattacks, including phishing and deepfake content, and that agentic AI carrying out multiple attack stages is an emerging trend. It says there are no widely accepted evaluation criteria for assessing offensive or defensive capabilities of generative AI. It presents four policy goals and 16 policy options.
events.plain: A US government watchdog report says AI can make cyberattacks bigger and faster, and can also help defenders. It lists options for policymakers.
events.exec: GAO says AI raises the reach of attacks such as phishing and deepfakes, and lists 16 policy options for government.
events.action: No action needed; for awareness.
events.impact: Policy report; no incident described.

validation.note: GAO's own product page (highlights and policy-goal tables) and CASRAI's summary read; the 70-page PDF text could not be extracted.

review.note: Compared report number, 20 Nov date, magnify/phishing/deepfake and agentic wording, no-evaluation-criteria sentence, 4 goals/16 options against GAO product page and CASRAI; all match

key_findings: AI lets threat actors magnify traditional attacks, making phishing and deepfake content higher quality and attacks more precise and faster; agentic AI carrying out several attack stages is an emerging trend.

GAO's page cites a June 2026 case of a threat actor using multiple AI agents to test malware against security products, and a February 2026 reported case of a low-skill actor using commercial generative AI to exploit stolen passwords on devices with weak passwords and no multi-factor authentication.
Defenders use machine learning and generative AI for tasks such as vulnerability scanning, finding flaws in source code and parsing large volumes of network data.
There are no widely accepted criteria for judging offensive or defensive AI capability, and generative AI adds new risks that expand the attack surface.
GAO sets out four policy goals and 16 policy options (guidance gaps, research gaps, governing AI tools through their lifecycle, workforce), presented as a menu rather than an exhaustive list.
recommendations: No formal recommendations were seen on GAO's report page; the 70-page PDF text was not read.

recommendations: Use Mandiant's published hardening guide and defence framework for machine-speed, LLM-enabled offensive tooling.

events.action: Enforce FIDO2 security keys for admins, alert on new passkey or MFA device enrolments and tenant-wide exports, and when remediating revoke all sessions, tokens, OAuth grants and rogue passkeys, not just passwords.

events.exec: One cloud breach became a launchpad for the next: stolen contacts made phishing believable. Phishing-resistant MFA and full session revocation are key.
events.plain: Google says a Russian spy group stole one US organisation's staff lists and files, then pretended to be its employees to trick and break into a second organisation.

key_findings: In late 2025 COLD RELIC used stolen Super Admin credentials, an MFA push-fatigue attack and a residential proxy near the victim to enter a US organisation's cloud tenant.
It downloaded the whole cloud drive, exported staff lists, ran a tenant-wide Customer Takeout and deleted Alert Center notifications to hide the intrusion.
Unrevoked attacker-enrolled passkeys let it get back in after password and session resets.
In 2026 it impersonated an employee of the first victim over an encrypted messaging app to phish Entra ID credentials at a second US organisation, then bulk-downloaded files.
GTIG observed new COLD RELIC phishing operations as recently as November 2026.
recommendations: Use phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn MFA and restrict and audit passkey and MFA device registrations.
Revoke all sessions, refresh tokens, OAuth grants, passkeys and backup codes when remediating, not just passwords.
Block or alert on admin logons from residential proxies and consumer ISPs.
Apply DLP rules to cloud storage for credentials, rosters and .pst files, and alert on tenant-wide exports and directory downloads.

events.summary: Mandiant and GTIG describe two linked intrusions by Russian espionage group COLD RELIC. In late 2025 it used a stolen Super Admin password and MFA fatigue to take a US organisation's entire cloud drive and staff directory. In 2026 it impersonated that organisation's staff over a messaging app to phish a second US organisation through Entra ID. GTIG saw new COLD RELIC phishing as recently as November 2026.

key_findings: GTIG found an exposed staging server hosting exploit_agent, a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with several frontier and local LLMs.

events.title: Kaspersky: AuditTeam ransomware crew uses OpsAgent framework and a signed driver to kill security tools
events.summary: Kaspersky describes AuditTeam, a ransomware-linked group that frames its demand as an audit and consulting fee and uses the OpsAgent framework, in C++ and Rust versions. Activity runs from January to October 2026, with infections in seven countries and its leak site claiming victims in seven further countries. It kills security tools using a signed Beijing Jiangmin driver.
events.plain: Researchers describe a ransomware group that disguises extortion as a consulting bill and switches off antivirus using a legitimately signed driver.
events.exec: A newly documented ransomware group with an EDR-killing driver; signed drivers can slip past some controls.
events.action: Check systems against Kaspersky's published hashes, domains, IP address and file paths (such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys); the report says shared CloudFront IPs are not reliable indicators on their own.

key_findings: Kaspersky says AuditTeam infected dozens of organisations, with victims seen in China, the Philippines, Senegal, Italy, Finland, Hong Kong and Russia, and its leak site lists victims in seven further countries.

The OpsAgent framework gives the operators file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture and network pivoting, and the ransom note demands an "Audit & Consulting fee" for a vulnerability report.
The campaign began in January 2026 and was active through October 2026 at a minimum; the page does not state how the group gets in.
OpsAgent was moved from C++ to Rust, and the Rust version uses CloudFront subdomains as C2 endpoints found through a GitHub repository.
An AV/EDR killer installs a driver disguised as a Beijing Jiangmin product and works from a kill list of about 220 process names.
recommendations: Check systems against the published stager and driver hashes, the two CloudFront domains, the IP address and the file paths such as syscache.dat and kvcore.sys.
Do not rely on the shared CloudFront IP addresses alone as indicators; the report says they cannot serve as reliable standalone IOCs.

validation.note: Original Kaspersky Securelist report read in full (read_depth full).

review.note: Compared title, summary, countries (dozens of organisations in seven countries; seven further on leak site), Jan-Oct 2026, Beijing Jiangmin signed driver, IOCs and CloudFront caveat with Securelist: match. Removed occurred_at 08:00Z, a time the page does not state.

events.title: Kaspersky: Retadup worm's revived servers now deliver CoffeeLoader
events.summary: Kaspersky says servers once used by the Retadup USB worm, disrupted by French police in 2019, now serve a new CoffeeLoader variant. The loader hides in a patched 7-Zip library and uses a packer that runs decryption on the GPU. Kaspersky says its products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems this year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, and it is unclear who runs the servers.
events.plain: An old USB worm that police shut down in 2019 is back and installing a newer malware loader that can bring in further malware. Kaspersky blocked infection attempts on about 15,000 systems.
events.exec: Removable drives can still carry malware that opens the door to later attacks, including from long-dead botnets.
events.action: Block autorun and restrict USB storage on endpoints, scan removable drives, and hunt for a patched 7z.dll running via rundll32.exe from %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%.

key_findings: A new CoffeeLoader variant uses a patched 7z.dll carrying a new version of the Armoury packer, which runs decryption on the GPU via OpenGL instead of OpenCL.
Domains used as Retadup command servers were re-registered about two years ago and first served SmokeLoader, then CoffeeLoader from early 2025.

Kaspersky products blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems in the first three quarters of the year, mostly in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia, far fewer than the 850,000 machines disinfected in 2019.
It is unclear whether the worm's author or another actor revived the servers.

key_findings: Victims are in Asia and Africa, mainly government; the worked example is two MeshCentral agent instances inside a Taiwanese organisation.
The entry point is unknown; evidence suggests reuse of an earlier infection, after which the MeshCentral agent was used for DLL sideloading and payload drops.
GitDoor receives commands and uploads results through GitHub accounts created between September 2024 and December 2025, and loads plug-ins and shellcode.
GraphDoor authenticates to Microsoft Graph, keeps encrypted victim data in SharePoint and loads plug-ins for keylogging, screenshots and proxy tunnels over Ably.
Kaspersky sees overlaps with Chinese-speaking FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle but says it cannot definitively attribute the activity.
recommendations: Treat the appearance of legitimate remote-management tools in the environment as suspicious.
Do not rely on network detection alone, since command traffic goes to trusted cloud APIs.
Use the indicators Kaspersky publishes in both parts for hunting.

events.impact: Correction requested from the Financial Services Commission; not a binding order on the banks.
events.summary: South Korea's Fair Trade Commission said on 23 November it reviewed 1550 bank and mutual savings bank terms made or revised in 2025 and found 73 unfair clauses, asking the Financial Services Commission to correct them, ZDNet Korea reports. According to the report, 9 banks and 1 savings bank had blanket clauses making customers responsible for all results of account or password misuse and excluding the bank's liability for losses including data loss.
events.plain: Korea's competition regulator found 73 unfair clauses in bank terms and asked the financial regulator to have them fixed. Some clauses make customers responsible for all results of account or password misuse.
events.exec: Korean banks may have to drop blanket clauses that put all account-misuse results on customers and excluded the bank's liability for losses such as data loss, per ZDNet Korea.
events.action: No action needed; for awareness.

events.title: South Korea plans higher minimum penalty for civil servants who leak personal information
events.impact: Proposed rule change; not yet in force.
events.summary: South Korea's Ministry of Personnel Management said on 19 November it will put an amendment to the enforcement rules of the civil servant disciplinary code out for pre-legislative notice from 20 November, Yonhap and Dailysecu report. No effective date is stated.
events.plain: South Korea proposes tougher minimum discipline, a pay cut, for civil servants who leak personal data, and for bosses who neglect oversight.
events.exec: Public-sector data leaks in Korea may carry heavier discipline, including for agency heads, once the rule takes effect.
events.action: No action needed; for awareness.

events.title: South Korea's FSC publishes draft digital asset law making operators liable for hacking losses even without fault
events.date_note: Both articles are dated 24 November and say the FSC presented the draft at a committee meeting that day.
events.geo_basis: the FSC, a South Korean government agency, as the articles state
events.summary: According to Financial News (Yonhap) and Kukmin Ilbo, South Korea's Financial Services Commission made public a government draft law on digital assets on 24 November. Under it, operators would in principle be liable for user losses from hacking or system failures even without intent or negligence, except where the user acted with intent or gross negligence. The draft also provides a basis for a punitive surcharge, capped at 10% of sales, for security failures.
events.plain: South Korea's financial regulator published a draft law under which crypto businesses would in principle have to compensate users for hacking losses even if the business was not at fault. It is not yet law.
events.exec: A draft Korean law would make digital asset operators liable for hacking losses without fault, with a punitive surcharge capped at 10% of sales for security failures.
events.action: No action needed; for awareness.

events.title: Phishing via Signal and Telegram targets European journalists and politicians, Le Monde reports
events.date_note: Date of the UNN and Slovo i Delo articles relaying Le Monde's investigation; neither gives an earlier day for the report. The campaign is said to have run since at least mid-October.
events.place: France (Le Monde's reporting; targets across Europe)
events.geo_basis: country of the reporting outlet and one named target (French MP); targets are in several European countries
events.summary: Citing Le Monde, UNN, Slovo i Delo, AzerNews and Meduza report a phishing campaign via Signal and Telegram against European journalists and politicians, running since at least mid-October; links led to fake pages. AzerNews says three Le Monde journalists received an invitation on 17 November. Meduza, citing Agentstvo, says Christo Grozev got a fake Google Meet link leading to a fake Telegram login page. Le Monde's sources link it to UNC5792.
events.plain: Fake messages from supposed acquaintances on Signal and Telegram are reportedly being used to steal logins from European journalists and politicians. The reports rely on Le Monde and its sources.
events.exec: Messaging-app phishing aimed at journalists and politicians is reported; the attribution comes from Le Monde's sources and has not been read at the original.
events.action: General advice: treat unexpected invitations to video calls or Telegram groups, even from known contacts, as suspect, and confirm them through another channel before clicking.
events.impact: Named targets in the reports include Christo Grozev, Bastian Obermayer, three Le Monde employees and French MP Eric Bothorel.

validation.note: UNN and Slovo i Delo both relay one Le Monde investigation, so this is a single source; Le Monde's original was not read (lemonde.fr could not be fetched on 23 Nov). Attribution to UNC5792 and an FSB unit is by Le Monde's sources and (per the articles) US authorities, not confirmed by a page read here. events.title: Study of 428 LLM API routers finds some inject malicious code and steal credentials
events.date_note: Date of the ITmedia report; the paper itself was submitted to arXiv on 9 April 2026.
events.summary: A paper by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and other institutions measured 428 third-party LLM API routers, 28 paid and 400 free. One paid and eight free routers actively injected malicious code, 17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials, and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
events.plain: Researchers found that some middleman services connecting AI coding agents to AI models altered commands, and some touched or drained decoy keys.
events.exec: Routing AI agent traffic through unvetted third parties exposes API keys, cloud credentials and code to theft or tampering.
events.action: Send agent traffic only to the model provider or a router you operate and trust, and rotate any keys that passed through an unvetted router.
events.impact: 9 of 428 routers injected code; 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials; one drained ETH from a researcher-owned key.

sources.name: arXiv: Your Agent Is Mine: Measuring Malicious Intermediary Attacks on the LLM Supply Chain

key_findings: The study scanned 428 routers, 28 paid and 400 free, and found one paid and eight free routers actively injecting malicious code.
Two routers used adaptive triggers such as waiting for 50 prior calls, limiting payloads to YOLO-mode sessions, or targeting only Rust and Go projects.
17 routers touched researcher-owned AWS canary credentials and one drained ETH from a researcher-owned private key.
Poisoning studies with a deliberately leaked OpenAI key and weakly configured decoys showed the routers' traffic exposed 99 credentials across 440 Codex sessions.
report.publisher: UC Santa Barbara and co-authors (arXiv paper)
recommendations: Use client-side mitigations such as a fail-closed policy gate, response-side anomaly screening and append-only transparency logging, which the paper says reduce exposure today.
Press for provider-backed response integrity, which the paper says is ultimately needed to secure the ecosystem.

validation.note: The paper's arXiv abstract and the start of its HTML text were read; ITmedia reports the same figures but words the AWS result more strongly ("misused"), so the paper's wording is used.

review.note: Paper abstract says 17 routers touched AWS canary credentials without saying free; only ITmedia says free. Removed 'free' from summary, impact, key finding. Counts 428/28/400, 1 paid + 8 free injecting, ETH checked against abstract and ITmedia.

events.title: Microsoft Agent Framework PyPI package compromised with credential stealer
events.summary: Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of the agent-framework package on PyPI were published on November 17 with a credential stealer that runs when Python starts, targeting cloud, GitHub and AI credentials and tokens. PyPI quarantined both; 1.26.0 is the last safe version. Italy's CSIRT (ACN) says the malware installed no OS-level persistence and downloaded no further payloads. Xakep.ru reports Microsoft said it made some repositories private during the investigation; the entry route is unknown.
events.plain: Two bad releases of a popular Microsoft AI package were uploaded to PyPI. Anyone who installed them may have had cloud and developer passwords and tokens stolen.
events.exec: A trusted package on an official Microsoft project carried a credential stealer; any build or developer machine that installed it may have exposed cloud access.
events.action: Wiz and CSIRT Italia advise pinning agent-framework to 1.26.0, checking lockfiles, CI logs and environments for 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, and rotating credentials and tokens exposed to any host that installed them.

key_findings: Malicious 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 ran a credential stealer at Python startup, even without importing the package.
Targets include Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face and OpenAI credentials and cloud identity tokens; data went to a webhook.site endpoint.
PyPI quarantined both releases; how the attacker got publish access is not known.
recommendations: Use 1.26.0 and rotate exposed credentials.

validation.note: Compared BleepingComputer with Wiz and Socket (independent vendor analyses): versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, November 17, .pth credential stealer, 1.26.0 safe; Wiz states both removed from PyPI about 21:30 UTC. Download figure rests on BleepingComputer only.

review.note: Action did not name its source: now attributed to Wiz and CSIRT Italia. Removed occurred_at 20:35 (no evidence quote). Added published days for BleepingComputer, Wiz and ACN. Versions, dates, targets, ACN no-persistence and Xakep repositories-private checked. Socket, ITmedia and Infobae not opened.

events.action: Tell developers to enter device codes only for sign-ins they started, review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations, and set Copilot CLI cloud session storage and memory to the least permissive setting that works.
events.exec: AI coding agents widen what a phished sign-in can reach, including code, past sessions and local commands; restrict agent session and memory settings.
events.plain: Microsoft tested how tricking a developer into typing a sign-in code could let a hacker control their AI coding assistant and read their private code. It has not seen this used in real attacks yet.

key_findings: In a controlled simulation, a test account approved a GitHub device-code request started by an attacker-controlled client using the public Copilot CLI client ID.
With that approval researchers could steer a remote-control-enabled Copilot CLI session to run a command, add misleading memory entries, read synced sessions and access private repositories.
The requested scopes included repo, read:user, read:org, gist and codespace, chosen by the client that starts the flow.
The technique applies to any public client supporting the device flow; Microsoft has not observed these four outcomes in the wild.
Microsoft cites earlier device-code phishing campaigns including Storm-2372 and EvilTokens, which it helped disrupt in September 2026.
recommendations: Approve device codes only for sign-ins you started yourself, even on the genuine github.com page.
Review GitHub Copilot CLI session storage and remote-control policy and choose the least permissive setting.
Review and revoke unexpected GitHub OAuth authorisations and limit repository access by role.
Review Copilot Memory for suspicious entries, and connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps for visibility.

events.summary: Microsoft researchers showed in a lab that a phished GitHub device-code approval for the Copilot CLI client could let an attacker steer a remotely controllable agent session, plant misleading memory entries, read cloud-synced sessions and reach private repositories. These are proof-of-concept results, not attacks seen in the wild. Microsoft added two Defender XDR detections for the email and Teams lures.
events.title: Microsoft: one phished device-code approval could let attackers steer AI coding agents

validation.note: Reviewed against the full original Microsoft Security Blog post; lab proof of concept only.

review.note: Four lab outcomes, not-in-the-wild statement and two Defender XDR detections match the Microsoft blog post.

events.action: Microsoft advises searching mail telemetry for the published sender domains and subject patterns, quarantining matches, and, for anyone who may have entered credentials, resetting the password and revoking sessions and tokens.
events.exec: Criminals are using a real outage to make scam emails convincing, raising the risk of stolen staff logins.
events.plain: Scammers are sending fake Microsoft 365 service notices that claim messages were held after an outage, according to Microsoft.

key_findings: Microsoft observed a high-volume phishing campaign on November 13 aimed at organisations in multiple sectors worldwide.
Emails use subjects like 'Outage' plus a random token and sender names posing as service-health notices, claiming four messages were held after a November 12 Exchange Online incident.
A 'RESTORE MESSAGES' button leads to a likely credential-phishing page; Microsoft has not confirmed credential capture.
Randomised subjects, recipient-specific tracking links and rotating sender domains are used to defeat simple pattern matching.
Microsoft has not attributed the campaign to a named actor or malware family.
recommendations: Search mail telemetry for the published sender domains, subject patterns and lure phrases, then quarantine and remove delivered copies.
Identify users who clicked using click, proxy and endpoint logs.
For anyone who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke sessions and tokens, verify MFA registrations and review inbox rules and OAuth grants.
Turn on Safe Links, Safe Attachments and zero-hour auto purge, and prefer phishing-resistant MFA.
Remind users that genuine service-health notices do not point to non-Microsoft sites; check the Microsoft 365 admin center.

events.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence describes a high-volume phishing campaign seen on November 13 that poses as Microsoft 365 service-health notices claiming messages were held after a November 12 Exchange Online incident. key_findings: The NCSC says it has seen a rise in AI-assisted attacks using agentic offensive frameworks, which are red-teaming tools repurposed for malicious use.
It says the weaknesses being exploited are not new and the tools give attackers no capability they lacked before; what changed is speed, persistence and low cost.
It says current frameworks are noisy, which makes them easier to detect, though future versions may be stealthier.

Targets named include credentials committed to code repositories, infrastructure-as-code misconfigurations, default credentials or missing authentication, API weaknesses, over-privileged credentials and flat networks.
recommendations: Keep an inventory of internet-facing assets, including forgotten legacy systems, and review it regularly.
Put services behind identity-aware proxies, firewalls or mutual TLS so only authenticated users can reach them.
Detect agent activity: look for bursts of requests, wide endpoint and parameter variety and high error rates, and retain correlated logs.
Patch internet-facing systems, audit identity and access settings for drift, and use pre-commit checks to stop secrets reaching repositories.
Apply rate limits per account, token or session at the API level, and consider honeytokens and decoy systems for high-confidence alerts.

events.exec: OpenSSL rates this QUIC memory flaw Low and says only applications that accept incoming streams are exposed; its default policy rejects peer-initiated streams.

Neither the researcher's pages nor the news report state exploitation in the wild.
recommendations: Upgrade to a fixed PHP release.
Interim: set session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 and restart PHP workers; this removes the easiest path, not the flaw.

events.action: Upgrade to a secure version of pip (the announcement says versions prior to v26.2.2 are affected), or upgrade Python to a version that rejects the compromised intermediates, or use hash pinning with a known-secure pip, as the announcement advises.

bundled certifi contains the compromised eMudhra certificates
recommendations: Upgrade pip
Upgrade Python to a version that rejects the compromised intermediates
Use hash pinning with a known-secure pip

events.action: Inventory every Java runtime, including bundled ones, and install the fixed releases (for example 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, 27.0.1.1), internet-facing systems first. See Rapid7's advisory for compensating controls where patching is not possible.
events.exec: A serious flaw in widely used Java versions, with a CISA alert urging immediate patching; fixes are available.
events.plain: Security firm Rapid7 and the US cyber agency warned of a serious flaw in recent versions of Java that could let outsiders run their own code. Oracle has released fixes.

key_findings: Memory corruption in the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot JVM; specially crafted input could allow unauthenticated remote code execution (CISA).
OpenJDK lists releases 17, 21, 25 and 27 as affected; Oracle fixed versions include 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1.

Rapid7 gives Oracle's CVSS v3.1 score as 8.1 (High); neither Rapid7 nor CISA reports exploitation in the wild. SecurityWeek (Nov 19) reports attempts: GreyNoise saw over 150 requests from five IP addresses and no successful intrusions on its sensors; Previdian logged nine attempts from six IPs and says its data cannot confirm compromise.
Researchers at Calif demonstrated unauthenticated RCE against several Java applications; Rapid7 says a reliable exploit needs significant extra work.
recommendations: Apply Oracle's November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update or the OpenJDK fixed releases, internet-facing systems first.
Inventory all JDKs and Java runtimes, including bundled ones; use compensating controls such as Base64 input validation where patching is not possible.

events.summary: Rapid7 and CISA warn of CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell), a memory corruption bug in the x86-64 HotSpot JVM Base64 decoder that could allow remote code execution; Oracle released fixes on November 17. SecurityWeek (Nov 19) reports GreyNoise saw over 150 matching requests from five IP addresses, with no successful intrusions seen on its sensors; Cisco, Siemens, Elastic and Red Hat issued advisories.
events.title: Rapid7 and CISA: critical Java flaw CVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) in Java 17 and later; Oracle patches released

events.action: Upgrade React and Next.js to fixed versions; until then strip or reject the x-middleware-subrequest header at the proxy or WAF, check logs for it and for /_next/image requests aimed at the metadata address, rotate every secret the server could reach, and enforce IMDSv2.
attack: T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
events.date_note: Date of OpenSourceMalware's published research; the repositories were created in waves from October 22.
events.exec: Stolen server secrets from Next.js sites are being committed to public GitHub repositories, so anyone can read them; unpatched sites are exposed.
events.geo_basis: GitHub, the platform hosting the campaign (no victim location stated)
events.plain: OpenSourceMalware reports a campaign that scans websites built with Next.js for known flaws and saves any stolen secrets in public GitHub repositories. Both flaws have had patches for months.

key_findings: OpenSourceMalware named the campaign React2STEAL and identified 45 repositories across 44 GitHub accounts running a scan.yml GitHub Actions workflow.

The pipeline tries React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182), the CVE-2025-29927 middleware bypass and an SSRF through /_next/image to cloud instance metadata, then collects environment variables, credentials and config files.
At least 1,281 unique victim hostnames across about 1,100 domains were found; results were still being committed about every 11 minutes on November 17.
OpenSourceMalware lists the threat actor as unknown and says it does not know whether the same operator ran the earlier wfx-loot campaign.
recommendations: Upgrade React and Next.js to fixed versions.
Strip or reject x-middleware-subrequest at the proxy or WAF until upgraded.
Rotate every secret the server could reach and enforce IMDSv2.

events.summary: OpenSourceMalware published research on November 18 on a campaign it named React2STEAL: 45 GitHub repositories across 44 accounts run scanners for React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) and CVE-2025-29927 and commit results to public repositories. It found at least 1,281 victim hostnames across about 1,100 domains. It lists the actor as unknown. GitGuardian's write-up says patches for both flaws have been available for months.

events.action: Verify WinRAR and other tools on your network are the publisher's signed copies; apply application allowlisting and code-signing checks, and alert on memory that is read, write and execute at once and on PNGs with truncated headers.
events.exec: Trusted programs can be rewritten into malware carriers whose fingerprint changes every run, so hash-based blocking is weak.
events.plain: Security firm ReversingLabs describes BubbleLoader, malware that edits ordinary programs like WinRAR so they secretly load other malware, and changes its fingerprint every time it runs.

key_findings: BubbleLoader patches the entry point of a benign program and appends two PNG files; the host then decrypts and reflectively loads a final payload in memory.
Hosts seen include WinRAR, x64dbg, Windows Media Player, a Firefox launcher and virtiofs; the post names no victims or sectors and the final payload varies by sample.
Earliest samples date from February 2026, with two activity clusters in mid-September and early October.

It overwrites padding bytes in the payload with timestamp-derived randomness on each run, so the in-memory hash changes every execution, and hooks RtlPcToFileHeader in ntdll so the payload can handle exceptions.
The second PNG is a fake with a truncated header, which ReversingLabs offers as a static detection signal; the post does not say how the altered programs reach victims.
recommendations: Enforce strict application allowlisting and code-signing verification, especially for common utilities such as WinRAR.
Have EDR alert on read-write-execute memory allocated with VirtualAlloc and on protection changes to the ntdll routine RtlPcToFileHeader.
Add static rules for embedded PNGs with a truncated header.
Rely on behavioural memory analysis and entry-point integrity checks, not only static payload hashes.

events.summary: ReversingLabs analysed BubbleLoader, a loader that rewrites a few instructions at a program's entry point and adds two PNG images to turn legitimate software, including WinRAR and Windows Media Player, into a carrier for other malware. It changes its payload's in-memory hash on every run. Samples date from February 2026, with activity clusters in September and October. Delivery method is not stated.
events.title: ReversingLabs: BubbleLoader turns WinRAR and other programs into malware carriers

validation.note: ReversingLabs original (highlights and intro read; full body only summarised) and Help Net Security's detailed write-up, which restates the vendor research.

review.note: Facts match ReversingLabs and Help Net Security; removed supply-chain tag as source states no supply-chain compromise

events.title: ReversingLabs links SSO vishing campaign to new extortion group Inception
events.date_note: Date of ReversingLabs' blog post; it says the campaign has been active since late October 2026.

key_findings: ReversingLabs says the Inception extortion group listed seven claimed victims on a Tor leak site; it describes these as unverified claims.
It says the group uses voice phishing to steal single sign-on credentials, and its lure domains have no mail DNS records, so they cannot receive email.

ReversingLabs identified 21 confirmed phishing domains running a kit that tailors pages to the target's identity provider, Okta or NetIQ; visitors who are not targets are redirected to the company's legitimate site.
Shared Cloudflare nameservers, NICENIC registrations and evening UTC registration patterns link the infrastructure, and ReversingLabs says they suggest further corporate targets beyond the leak site.
It says the activity has run since late October 2026.
recommendations: Require phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2 keys, passkeys or origin-bound authenticators, plus managed device controls and alerts on unexpected MFA changes.
Train employees and help desks to verify urgent legal or compliance sign-in requests, and verify identity before resetting credentials or MFA.
Monitor new domain registrations and certificate transparency logs for brand-plus-legal naming, and block suspicious domains at DNS and web proxies.
Hunt DNS, proxy and identity logs from 21 October 2026 onward; if targeting is confirmed, revoke sessions and reset credentials.

events.place: United States (no victim location stated; pin at country)
events.geo_basis: country; the report names no single location

Several could allow remote code execution in some scenarios, notably where attacker-controlled patterns are compiled.
Maintainers say they are aware of proof-of-concept code that shows remote code execution for some; GBHackers says the disclosure reported no active exploitation.
Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end of life and will not be fixed.
recommendations: Upgrade to a fixed release.
Avoid compiling attacker-controlled regular expressions.

events.summary: SOCRadar reports that a French-speaking operator it calls BabidiGhost spent nine days in November 2026 targeting European banks, insurers, payment providers and municipalities through a jailbroken AI agent, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland. According to SOCRadar, the agent held 23 archives, about 8.6 GB, belonging to more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies, and an unpatched Metabase instance vulnerable to CVE-2023-38646 let it into one victim. Victims are not named.
events.plain: Security firm SOCRadar says one attacker used a jailbroken AI agent to go after European banks, insurers and town councils, and that it held about 8.6 GB of files from public bodies.
events.exec: SOCRadar documents an AI agent doing intrusion work for one operator; an unpatched Metabase server was one way in.
events.action: SOCRadar advises hunting logs for 5 to 17 November 2026, closing internet-exposed analytics tools, storage interfaces, test portals and API docs, and keeping secrets out of application runtime environments.

evidence.quote: 23 archives, about 8.6 GB, belonging to more than 13 municipalities and 10 other public bodies
a French-speaking operator who spent nine days in November 2026 targeting European banks, insurers, payment providers and municipalities through a jailbroken AI agent

key_findings: A French-speaking operator SOCRadar calls BabidiGhost used a jailbroken AI agent for nine days, typing 1,801 plain-language orders that the agent relayed as 5,779 requests to its model.

More than 50 organizations and datasets were targeted, mostly in Belgium, France and Switzerland; of 14 analysed in depth, two were breached, three partly breached, four resisted and five saw reconnaissance only.

Entry came through ordinary weaknesses, not zero-days: an internet-facing Metabase instance vulnerable to CVE-2023-38646, a readable container secret, a weak admin password on a shared storage server and an unauthenticated API route.
MFA, IP allowlisting and server-side validation stopped the agent where they were in place.
SOCRadar says the model API key was revoked on 14 November 2026 and deployed implants checked in until 15 November.
recommendations: Hunt logs for the report's indicators from 5 to 17 November 2026 and check for the implant artifacts SOCRadar describes.
Inventory internet-facing tools, storage interfaces, test portals and API docs, and treat anything reachable without authentication as already exposed.
Keep secrets out of application runtime environments.
Add authentication, rate limits and account-enumeration protections to sign-in flows and SMS or email functions.
Monitor for unexplained traffic to model-provider APIs and the Telegram bot API.

validation.note: Primary source: SOCRadar's own report (the investigating firm), read in part; GBHackers relays it. No victim is named and no victim statement was read.

review.note: Compared date, nine days, 23 archives/8.6 GB, Metabase CVE, unnamed victims, recommendations against SOCRadar report

events.summary: Varonis Threat Labs describes TheMailer, a self-hosted phishing platform sold for a lifetime licence of about $3,000 to $6,000. events.title: TU Berlin researchers bypass firmware-TPM lockout to crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs (CVE-2026-43613)
events.summary: TU Berlin researchers reset the lockout counter of firmware TPMs by replacing the flash chip, letting an attacker with physical access guess Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs far faster. A 6-digit BitLocker PIN fell in 236 tries. AMD tracks it as CVE-2026-43613 (CVSS 5.1) with fixes planned November 2026 to February 2027; Intel reports no flaw in its component. Lab only.
events.plain: Researchers showed that someone holding a laptop can reset its PIN-guess limit by swapping a chip, then crack the PIN in days instead of years.
events.exec: Requires physical access and hardware modification, so the risk is for lost or stolen laptops; no exploitation reported.
events.action: Use long alphanumeric PINs or TPM plus startup key for BitLocker on high-risk laptops, and apply AMD firmware updates as they ship.

key_findings: Flash-chip replacement resets the 32-try lockout on firmware TPMs.
4-digit Hello PIN worst case 40 hours versus 69 days; 6-digit BitLocker PIN 20 days versus 19 years.
AMD fixes planned Nov 2026 to Feb 2027; Intel and Microsoft issued no CVE.
recommendations: Stronger PINs; apply AMD firmware updates.

validation.note: Read via fetch agent; cites arXiv 2611.18126, AMD SB-7079 and Intel notice, not opened.

review.note: THN Nov 18: CVE-2026-43613 CVSS 5.1, 236 tries, AMD fix Nov-Feb 2027, Intel no flaw, lab only match.

events.action: Log and inspect QUIC traffic or block outbound UDP 443 so it falls back to inspectable TCP. Patch Exchange and web servers, review accounts holding the ApplicationImpersonation role and audit Group Policy logon scripts for changes.
events.actor: TGR-STA-0049 (also REF7707, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon)
events.exec: Espionage tools now hide in HTTP/3 traffic that many network monitors skip; unpatched Exchange servers remain the way in.
events.plain: Researchers found a spying group breaking into government networks in Southeast Asia through unpatched email servers and hiding its remote-control traffic inside a newer web protocol many security tools do not inspect.

key_findings: Targets are Southeast Asian government entities; one decoy PDF imitates a Myanmar election commission document, though victim countries are not confirmed.
Entry is through unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers to plant web shells, with phishing using decoy PDFs and DLL sideloading as a second route.
PerfectPioneer, a Go tool with six variants, uses HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 depending on the variant (one variant uses HTTP/3 with HTTP/2 fallback); two variants add a blocklist of dangerous commands.
KUKURAT loads at least 12 modules for keylogging, screenshots, lateral movement and tunnelling, and creates decoy network, registry and file activity.
Activity spans about nine months and included mass mailbox permission changes on Exchange and credential theft from a domain controller.
recommendations: Log and inspect QUIC traffic, or block outbound UDP 443 so HTTP/3 falls back to inspectable TCP.
Audit SYSVOL and Group Policy for unauthorised logon script changes.
Create behavioural rules for rundll32.exe loading comsvcs.dll, including ordinal-based calls.
Review accounts with the ApplicationImpersonation role and watch Exchange logs for repeated Add-MailboxPermission FullAccess grants.

events.summary: Unit 42 describes about nine months of intrusions into Southeast Asian government networks by a group it tracks as TGR-STA-0049. The attackers entered through unpatched Microsoft Exchange and web servers, then deployed two custom remote access tools, PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT, that talk to their controllers over HTTP/3. KUKURAT also generates decoy activity to hide what it is doing.
